Peter Melius
pē'-ter mā'-li-us
n. (Peter Melius Juhasz, c. 1532–1572, bishop of Debrecen, organiser of the Hungarian Reformed Church)
Greek Petros, a rock; Hungarian Juhasz, a shepherd, latinised Melius.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Peter Melius was the organiser of the Reformed Church in Hungary and for fourteen years bishop of Debrecen, the city which became and remains its capital. Trained at Wittenberg, he returned convinced on the Reformed rather than the Lutheran side of the sacramental question, and set about giving the Hungarian churches a confession, a government and a defence. He presided over a succession of synods — Tarcal, Torda, Debrecen — which adopted the Second Helvetic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism, established presbyterial oversight under superintendents, and settled the order of worship. His hardest fight was against the antitrinitarians: Francis David, once his ally, carried the Transylvanian church into Unitarianism, and Melius met him in the great public disputations of 1566 and 1568 before King John Sigismund, contending for the deity of Christ and the Trinity from Scripture alone. He published over forty works in Hungarian, including a catechism, confessions, and part of a Bible translation, and he died at Debrecen in 1572 worn out at forty. “I and my Father are one” (Joh 10:30) was the text the disputations turned on.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the Trinity as the union of three persons in one Godhead, and a superintendent as one who has the oversight and charge of something.

expand to see more

TRIN'ITY, n. The union of three persons in one Godhead.

SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.

DISPUTA'TION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition.

Modern Corruption

Debrecen's bishop, who gave Hungary its Reformed order and fought the antitrinitarians.

expand to see more

The error Melius faced in Transylvania is the one that always follows a successful appeal to Scripture against tradition: having set aside the councils, a man asks why he should keep the creed they wrote, and concludes that the Trinity is a Greek addition. Francis David made precisely that argument, and he made it as a Reformer.

The principle to recover is that the Trinity is not an inference from councils but the plain speech of Scripture. The commission names the three in one name (Mat 28:19), the apostolic benediction names all three (2Co 13:14), and the Son says outright, “I and my Father are one” (Joh 10:30). A church that cannot say this has not simplified its faith; it has lost its object of worship.

"“baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19) — his argument from the commission."
